reason: The court rejected the non-registration objection by holding that no mandatory registration provision was needed to sue on the trust receipt.
The court applied the account-stated principle that silence as to credited entries amounted to admission of their correctness.
The statement omits the court's material limits that the part payment must be on account of the debt and reflected in the stated account or acknowledgement.
The court only held that this plaintiff was not barred from bringing this particular deed-of-gift action, not that plaintiffs may file new actions at any time during earlier proceedings.
The no-res-judicata holding depended on the plaintiff being a defendant in the divorce action, having already filed the separate action, and having reserved forfeiture rights.
The extraction misreads the phrase 'as seen from' as physical-boundary reasoning when the court was listing factual acts supporting prescriptive title.
Continued possession after the owner's death and after the widow left was one of the court's stated facts supporting ouster and prescriptive title.
Planting coconuts and enjoying produce was treated by the court as one of the overt acts supporting adverse possession and prescription.
The court expressly applied the Notaries Ordinance duty to state whether consideration passed before the notary as a factor undermining the deed.
The appeal turned in part on the trial judge's failure to evaluate the evidence and the constructive-trust issue properly.
The statement drops the Ceiling on Housing Property Law tenant-purchase context and the qualification that the applicant must still be a tenant and the premises still a house at the decisive stage.
The statement wrongly says any cultivator is covered, while the court's rule was limited to paddy land let to a cultivator under an oral or written agreement.
The court held that tenancy rights could be ceded only under the statutory procedure and that non-compliant cessation was null and void.
The court rejected the use of the interpretation section to strip a tenant cultivator's rights solely because he became a usufructuary mortgagee.
The statement is a meta-comment on a truncated extraction and is contradicted by the full held passage, which expressly discusses the High Court order.
The court held that default in filing a statement of claim did not prevent the first defendant from relying on the plaintiff's pleaded title.
The court held that the first defendant could not be deprived of his pleaded rights by a private settlement among other parties.
The court stated the partition-action compromise rule with the required prior investigation of each party's title and rights.
The court held that a settlement or compromise must strictly comply with Civil Procedure Code sections 91 and 408.
The court did not merely say a court can investigate title; it imposed title investigation and satisfaction as preconditions to a valid partition compromise.
The statement overstates the holding because the court allowed Civil Procedure Code use for writ formalities while requiring Partition Law sections 52 and 53 for delivery of possession.
The court expressly preserved use of the Civil Procedure Code for formal execution matters while excluding it for delivery-of-possession applications.
The court relied on the first defendant's failure to deny the spousal relationship and basis of heir liability in the pleadings.
The judgment concerned liability through an alleged legal representative or heir of the estate, not a broad personal liability of any heir for the deceased's acts.
The statement omits the court's limiting context that 'heir' was being read broadly in the caption and legal-representative setting under the Civil Procedure Code.
